e.t: Abarin, also rendered Avarin, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Deuteronomy 32:49. The available lexical meaning identifies the name itself, but without the surrounding verse text, its specific contextual significance cannot be explained here. Its role is therefore to identify a named entity in that passage, not to express a broad concept used throughout the Greek Old Testament.

This word means “cruelly,” describing an action done in a harsh, merciless, or deliberately harmful manner. As an adverb, it tells how someone acts rather than naming a person, object, or action by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 15:2. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense is an act carried out with cruelty.

This word is a proper name rendered “Azob” or “Azov.” It does not describe an action, quality, or object in general; it identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs once in the LXX, at 1 Samuel 7:14. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its specific referent cannot be described more precisely, but its basic function is that of a place or personal name as determined by context.

Akipha, also rendered Akifa, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a descriptive word or action term, so its basic meaning is the person’s name rather than a quality or idea. This name appears once in the Greek text, at Ezra 2:51, in a list of people associated with the return from exile. The surrounding verse text is not included here, so the person’s specific role cannot be explained further from this word alone.

Aloel, also given as “Alil,” is a personal name identifying an individual in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general description, action, or quality, but a name used to distinguish one person. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Genesis 46:14. Since no verse text or broader context is available here, its normal meaning is simply the individual’s name rather than a word expressing a separate concept.

Amorraia, also rendered “Amorrea,” is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Kings 11:1. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain whether it identifies a person, people, or place in that passage. Its precise reference therefore belongs to the context of 1 Kings 11:1, while its basic lexical function is simply a proper name.

This noun means “effrontery”: bold, shameless disrespect or behavior that ignores what is proper. It describes an attitude or action marked by audacious disregard, rather than simple confidence or courage. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), in Sirach 25:22. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central meaning remains a brazen lack of proper restraint or respect.

ἀναφωνέω means “call out”—to speak or cry aloud so that the words are heard. It is a verb describing an audible act of calling, rather than a quiet thought or private statement. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times in five verses: four in 1 Chronicles and once in 2 Chronicles. Its precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains an outward, audible call.

This Greek LXX verb means “lead off” or “lead away”: it describes taking someone or something from one place to another. It can refer to physical removal, guidance, or being carried away, depending on the sentence. The word occurs 36 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, so it is a recurring action word rather than a rare expression. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on who is leading and what is being taken. [p03:word:lxx:L701324:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L701324:occurrences]

This Greek LXX verb means to “marvel much at a,” expressing strong amazement or wonder toward someone or something. It describes an intense response rather than a simple notice or interest. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus: once in Daniel and three times in Sirach. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is deep astonishment. It functions as an action word describing what a person does when greatly amazed.

This verb means to release someone when a ransom or payment has been made. It describes liberation obtained through a required payment, rather than simple permission to leave. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Exodus and Zephaniah, so its central idea is specific and focused: a person is freed by means of ransom. The precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage. [P03 identity; P03 occurrences]

This verb means “horribly tortured,” describing severe and dreadful physical suffering. It refers to the experience of being tormented in an extreme way, rather than simply facing difficulty or pain. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs only once, in 2 Maccabees 9:7, so its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s direct meaning is clear even though no broader usage pattern is available.

This word means “silver,” referring to the metal used as a material or valuable possession. It is a noun, so it names the substance itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs 11 times, appearing in passages from Exodus, Ezra, Proverbs, Isaiah, Daniel, and Wisdom. Its central meaning remains consistent across these uses: silver as a recognized material of worth and practical use.

Arphad, also rendered Arfath, is a proper name for a place mentioned in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a geographical name preserved in the biblical text. This name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament: twice in 2 Kings and once in Jeremiah. Because the available information identifies the name but does not provide the surrounding verse text, its particular significance in each passage must be understood from the context of those passages.

This Greek LXX noun means “ruling priest,” describing a priest who holds governing authority among priests. It identifies an office or person rather than an action or quality. The word occurs 40 times in the Greek LXX corpus, including the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so it is used across several settings involving priestly leadership. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains a priest with authority over others.

Atarōth, rendered “Ataroth,” is a proper name rather than a common word with a general descriptive meaning. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a named place or locality in Israel’s territorial and genealogical records. It occurs five times, in Numbers, Joshua, and 1 Chronicles, and is consistently rendered “Ataroth.” Its exact significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and list in which the name appears.

This word means “kind of locust,” referring to a particular type of locust named among the creatures discussed in Leviticus. It is a noun, so it identifies the insect rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Leviticus 11:22. The word’s precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the name of a specific locust variety.

Achor is a proper name, rendered “Achōr” or “Akhor,” rather than a common word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times in four separate verses: twice in Joshua and once each in Isaiah and Hosea. Because it is a name, its basic function is to identify Achor; the particular significance of that name in any verse must be understood from the surrounding passage.

This adjective describes speech that is obscure—words whose meaning is not readily clear to the hearer. It is a descriptive term for the manner or clarity of speaking, rather than the name of a person or thing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ezekiel 3:5. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is speech that is difficult to understand.

Barachiel is a proper name, also given as Varakhil. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs twice, both times in Job: Job 32:2 and Job 32:6. Without the surrounding verse text, its personal significance cannot be explained further here; its basic lexical function is simply to designate this named individual.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Bēthmaalōn” or “Vithmaalon.” It functions as a specific designation rather than a general description, so its meaning is chiefly the identity of the named referent. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at Judges 9:6. Without the verse text or an additional lexical definition, its precise referent cannot be explained further here; its established sense is the proper name itself.

This noun means “ditch”: a hollow or excavated place in the ground. It refers to a physical depression that can serve as a trench, channel, or pit, depending on the surrounding passage. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 12 times across 9 verses, including passages from Samuel, Kings, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. The basic image is a sunken place in the earth, while the precise use in any verse depends on its immediate context.

Gasin is a proper name preserved as “Gasin” in the Greek Old Testament. As a name, it identifies a particular person, place, or other named entity rather than expressing an action or quality, though the supplied information does not specify which kind. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Joshua 18:15. Its precise referent must therefore be determined from the surrounding verse and passage, not from the name alone.

This Greek LXX verb means “get old”: it describes becoming advanced in age or growing old. It is an action word, focusing on the process of aging rather than simply naming an old person. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including passages about Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Joshua, and Naomi. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains the same: to grow or become old.

Gōthi, also written Gothi, is a proper name identifying a person. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a personal designation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 9:4. Because the available information gives the name and reference but not the verse text, its specific family connection or role cannot be stated here. The name’s precise significance in that passage belongs to its surrounding context.

This Greek LXX noun means “fear” or “alarm”—the inward response of being troubled, frightened, or suddenly aware of danger. It names an emotional condition rather than an action, so it describes what a person feels when confronted by something threatening or overwhelming. The word occurs five times in the LXX material, all in 2 Maccabees, showing a focused use for fearful distress or alarm. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

The verb means “pronounce”: to speak or announce something aloud. It describes making a message known through speech rather than merely holding it privately. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs nine times, so it is a recurring action word rather than a rare technical term. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on what is being spoken and to whom, but its central idea remains verbal declaration.

This Greek LXX verb means to examine. It describes the act of looking into something closely in order to understand or assess it. The word functions as an action, focusing attention on the process of careful examination rather than on a person, object, or quality. It occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus: once in Sirach 51:19 and once in 2 Maccabees 2:28. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding context.

This verb means “dawn”: it describes the coming of daylight or the beginning of day. It is an action word, focusing on daybreak rather than on a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Judges 19:26. That single occurrence establishes its basic sense, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain its precise force in that passage.

This Greek LXX verb means to acquire possessions—to obtain and come to have property or goods. It describes the act of gaining possessions rather than merely having them. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 34:10, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains straightforward: obtaining possessions or property.

The word means “compound.” It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person, place, or thing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, all in Proverbs. Because the actual verse wording and surrounding context are not available here, its precise force in each passage cannot be explained further; the central lexical sense remains the action described as “compound.”

Ekkēs is a proper name, also rendered Ekkis, identifying an individual rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twice, both times in 1 Chronicles: at 1 Chronicles 11:28 and 1 Chronicles 27:9. Its basic meaning is therefore the person’s name itself; the surrounding verse is needed to identify what details are given about the named individual.

This Greek LXX verb means “wash out”: to cleanse something by washing it away or out. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Isaiah 4:4, so its normal meaning is clear but its broader range of use cannot be measured from repeated occurrences. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and context. [p03:word:lxx:L704288:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L704288:occurrences] [p01:word:lxx:L704288:reference:0]

Emak is a proper name, used to identify a specific person, place, or other named referent rather than to express a general quality or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears only once, in Joshua 13:19. The lexical evidence preserves the name itself but does not establish from the name alone what kind of referent Emak identifies; the surrounding verse supplies that detail.

The LXX adjective “straitened” describes a person or condition marked by restriction, hardship, or lack. It points to circumstances in which there is little room or provision, rather than naming an action. This word occurs 23 times in the LXX corpus, with most occurrences in Proverbs. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is a narrowed or difficult state.

This word means “precept”: an instruction, rule, or command that directs a person’s conduct. As a noun, it refers to something given to be followed rather than to an action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, in passages from Job and Isaiah. Its basic sense is a clearly stated requirement or directive, while the surrounding verse determines who gives it and what obedience to it involves.

This verb means “it is permissible”: something is allowed, lawful, or within what may be done. It expresses permission rather than merely describing an action. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs seven times across Ezra, Esther, 1 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. The precise action being permitted depends on the sentence and surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies what may rightly be done or accepted.

This verb means “exorcise” or “put on oath.” It describes an action involving either the expulsion of a spiritual power or the placing of someone under an oath. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 24:3. Because the word appears only there and the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that sentence depends on the passage’s context; its basic lexical sense remains the act of exorcising or putting on oath.

This noun means “rising up,” referring to movement or a return upward. It presents the idea of getting up, ascending, or coming back up rather than remaining down. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains the act or movement of rising. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that corpus rather than merged with similarly rendered words elsewhere.

This Greek LXX noun means a covering or wrapper: something placed over or around another thing. It names a physical covering rather than an action or quality. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament translation, in Judges and Ezekiel, showing this ordinary object-related sense across both books. Its exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains something used to cover, wrap, or conceal. References include Judges 4:18 and Ezekiel 13:18, 21.

This Greek LXX verb means “fall on/upon.” It describes something or someone coming down onto another person or thing, or arriving upon it. The wording can therefore express physical falling, a force coming against someone, or an arrival that overtakes them, depending on the sentence. It occurs 43 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its central idea is repeated across several kinds of passages. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means “visit” or “inspect.” It describes going to someone or something with purposeful attention, whether to check its condition, examine it, or attend to it. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person or quality. It occurs 148 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, showing that it is used broadly for attentive visitation and examination. The precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “workwoman,” referring to a woman who works. It identifies a female worker rather than describing a specific occupation or task by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 6:8. The word therefore carries a straightforward occupational meaning: a woman engaged in work. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points plainly to a working woman.

This adjective means “of wool” or “woollen,” describing something made from or associated with wool. It is a specific material word rather than a term for a person, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Leviticus 13, where the subject concerns cloth and related materials. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the noun it describes, but its basic meaning remains consistent: connected with wool or made of wool.

This noun means “evening,” the latter part of the day as daylight gives way to night. In the Greek Old Testament, it can identify a time of day and may mark when an event, instruction, or appointed action occurs. The word appears 119 times in the LXX corpus, from Genesis through 4 Maccabees, showing regular use for this ordinary period of the day. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek LXX verb means to benefit—to do good for someone or bring help and advantage. It describes an action rather than a person or quality, so it answers the question of what someone does for another. The word appears 10 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, including Psalms, Esther, Wisdom, and the Maccabean books. Its precise emphasis in any individual verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains actively doing good or providing benefit.

This noun refers to good repute—an honored name or favorable standing—and can also mean glory. It describes the esteem or distinction a person possesses rather than an action they perform. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, it occurs three times, each in a different verse. Its precise emphasis can depend on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains recognized worth, honor, or an esteemed reputation.

This adverb means “strongly” or “mightily,” describing an action carried out with great strength, force, or power. It tells how something is done rather than naming a person, thing, or action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, with the same central idea throughout. Its wording can describe powerful action in a broad sense, while the surrounding sentence determines exactly what is being done forcefully.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person named “Ēlia” or “Ilia.” It is not a general description, action, or quality, but a personal designation used in the Greek Old Testament and related writings. The name occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus: once each in 1 Chronicles, Ezra, and Sirach. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific reference cannot be identified more precisely here.

Thamna is a proper name used in the Greek Old Testament to identify a named entity; the name itself does not express a broader descriptive sense such as an action or quality. It occurs eight times in the LXX corpus, appearing in Genesis and later in 1 and 2 Chronicles. Since the verse texts are not included, its particular referent in any occurrence must be determined from that passage.

Thekōi, also given as Theki, is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 1 Chronicles 11:28. The available information identifies the name and its occurrence, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain whether it refers to a person, place, or another named subject. Its precise referent therefore depends on reading the verse and its surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means to “lament” or “wail”—to express deep grief openly. It describes audible mourning rather than a quiet feeling alone. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament passages represented here, appearing in 2 Samuel and 2 Chronicles. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains an outward cry or expression of sorrow. [p03:word:lxx:L706307:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L706307:occurrences]

This word is a proper name, rendered “Iesbakasa” or “Iezvakasa.” It identifies a named individual in the Greek Old Testament rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs twice in the LXX, both times in 1 Chronicles 25, at verses 4 and 24. The available information establishes the name’s identity and spelling variants, but does not provide a separate lexical meaning for the name itself.

This noun means “appeasement”: an action or provision intended to remove offense and restore favor. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings, it describes the idea of addressing what has caused displeasure rather than ignoring it. The word occurs six times in this LXX corpus, across Leviticus, Numbers, Psalms, Ezekiel, Amos, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This noun means “going down” or “descent,” describing movement from a higher place or position to a lower one. It occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament represented here, both times in Ecclesiastes. The word’s basic sense is directional: it points to the act or process of descending rather than to a person or object. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and larger context, which are not included here.

Kasōn, also rendered Kason, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it appears once, in 2 Samuel 23:13. Because it functions as a personal name, its meaning is primarily identification: it names a particular person or figure in the biblical account. The surrounding verse is needed to explain that individual’s role, since the name itself does not express a further idea.

This adjective means “descending,” describing something that moves or comes downward. It presents direction rather than naming a person, object, or action by itself, so the surrounding sentence supplies what is descending. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 10:6. Because the verse text is not included, its precise reference cannot be expanded into a fuller verse-level description. Its central sense remains the movement or direction from a higher position toward a lower one.

This verb means “break apart”: to separate something into pieces or cause it to lose its unity. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word therefore points to decisive separation or fracturing, not merely movement or change. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 19:12. Its basic lexical sense remains “break apart,” while the precise force of that action depends on the surrounding verse context.

This noun refers to settling something into an established order or appointing someone to a position. Its central idea is the act of putting matters or people into a proper, assigned arrangement. The word occurs once in the Greek Septuagint corpus, in Wisdom 12:12. Because the available wording gives the basic lexical sense but not the surrounding verse text, the precise force in that passage depends on its context. The meaning remains focused on settling or appointing rather than on a general state of disorder or change.

This Greek LXX verb means “dominate” or “hit on the head.” It describes forceful action, either exercising control over someone or striking the head. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 32:8. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic sense points to forceful control or a blow directed at the head.

This LXX noun means “tempest,” referring to a powerful, turbulent storm at sea or on land. It describes a force of nature marked by violent movement and danger, rather than a person or action. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this LXX corpus, including several occurrences in Jonah and Wisdom. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means “have a sick head-ache,” describing the experience of suffering from a painful or unwell head. It refers to a physical condition rather than an object or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Psalms and Isaiah. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning centers on having a sick headache.

This Greek LXX verb means “knock”: to strike against a door or another surface, usually to announce someone’s presence or seek entry. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or abstract idea. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Judges 19:22 and once in Song of Songs 5:2. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and scene, but its basic meaning remains the physical act of knocking.

This word refers to a pot or cauldron, a vessel used for holding or heating something. It is a noun, so it names the object itself rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Leviticus 11:35. The word’s basic meaning is therefore specific and concrete: a cooking or heating vessel. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the object being described there.

Kōla, also written Kola, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. Its exact referent must be identified from the surrounding passage, since the lexical information gives the name but not whether it designates a person, place, or other named entity. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times across six verses, from Leviticus through Isaiah. It remains a distinct Greek LXX name and should not be treated as an ordinary translation term.

Maath is a proper name, identifying a person named Maath in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs twice in the Greek LXX, both times in 2 Chronicles: once in 2 Chronicles 29:12 and once in 2 Chronicles 31:13. The name itself does not describe an action, quality, or idea; it functions as a personal designation. Understanding the person’s particular role requires the wording and surrounding context of each passage.

This proper name means “Madianitēs” or “Mathianitis” and identifies a Madianite. It is a name or designation for someone belonging to the Madianite people, rather than a word describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Numbers 10:29. The reference identifies where the term appears, but the precise role it plays there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This verb means to persevere—to continue steadily rather than give up. It describes sustained effort or endurance, emphasizing persistence over time. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 8:26. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its ordinary meaning is the determined continuation of an action or effort despite difficulty or delay.

This word means to smile: it describes the act of smiling. As a verb, it describes an action rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 21:20. That reference identifies its only occurrence, but without the verse text it cannot establish whether the smile is friendly, mocking, joyful, or connected with another circumstance. Its basic meaning remains simple and concrete: someone smiles. The exact force in that verse must be understood from the surrounding wording.

This Greek LXX verb describes leading someone onward or causing a change of course. Its basic sense is “lead after; change course,” so it can express movement that follows a prior direction or a turning toward a different one. It occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented here, across historical and wisdom writings. The exact force in any verse depends on who or what is being led and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX noun means “repentance” or “regret”—a change of heart marked by sorrow over what has been done. It can describe the feeling of wishing an action had not occurred, or the turning associated with recognizing wrong. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including one occurrence rendered “regret” and another rendered “repentance.” Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This word functions as a noun—a naming word for a person, thing, place, or idea. The available lexical description identifies its part of speech but does not give a more specific meaning, so its exact referent must be understood from the sentence where it appears. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek books represented here, it occurs 18 times, from Exodus through Susanna. It is therefore a recurring noun, but its particular sense cannot be narrowed further without the surrounding verse.

This word means “habitat”: a place where living beings dwell. It refers to an inhabited setting or living place, rather than to a single person or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 48 times, showing that it is used across many passages to speak of places understood as inhabited. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word describes someone or something as “notable”—recognized as worthy of attention or distinguished in some way. It can function as an adjective describing a person, group, or thing, and its related noun use can identify one who is notable. The word appears 20 times in the Greek LXX corpus, across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what person or thing the surrounding passage presents as distinguished.

This Greek LXX noun means “vision”: something seen or presented to sight. It names a visual experience or sight, rather than an action or a person. The word occurs 42 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, with many occurrences in Daniel and several in Isaiah, where it identifies what is seen. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “charge”: to move forward forcefully or rush toward something. It describes purposeful, energetic movement rather than merely being present or traveling slowly. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 15 times, including passages from Genesis, Joshua, Isaiah, and 2 Maccabees. The surrounding wording determines whether the charge is by people, animals, or an advancing force, but the central idea remains a strong, sudden movement toward a destination or objective.

Our, also rendered Ur, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person named in three separate verses: Numbers 31:8, Joshua 13:21, and 1 Chronicles 11:35. The name appears once in each of those verses, so its precise identity and significance depend on the surrounding passage. It is best understood simply as the personal name Our or Ur.

This word refers to a concubine or mistress—a woman recognized in that social and household role. It is a noun, naming the person rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 19:17. The word’s basic meaning identifies a woman connected to a man in this particular relationship; the precise force of the reference depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This verb means “talk at random”: speaking in a disordered, unfocused, or haphazard way rather than expressing a clear, deliberate message. It describes an action, so it tells what someone does with speech, not the name of a person or thing. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Psalms 43:17. The precise force in that verse depends on its surrounding wording, but the basic idea remains speech that lacks orderly direction.

This Greek verb means to “goad” or “irritate”—to provoke or stir someone toward a response. It can describe conduct that pricks, angers, or presses another person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 48 times, so its basic sense appears across many passages rather than belonging to one narrow setting. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on provoking anger, urging action, or inciting offense.

This noun means “mother-in-law,” referring to a woman related to someone through marriage. It names the mother of a person’s husband or wife, rather than a biological mother. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 13 times in 12 verses, with most occurrences in Ruth, where the word identifies the family relationship between Naomi and Ruth. Its meaning remains straightforward and relational; the surrounding verse determines what that relationship means in the immediate situation.

This adverb means “round about” or “all round,” describing something situated, moving, or arranged around a person, place, or thing. It adds a surrounding or encompassing sense to the sentence rather than naming an object itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 21 times across 21 verses, so its basic idea is used in varied settings while remaining spatial and direct. The exact force in any verse depends on what it modifies and the surrounding wording.

This LXX noun means a “mistake” or “transgression”—a wrong act or failure that violates what is right. It names wrongdoing as a noun, rather than describing an action in progress. In the Greek Old Testament collection represented here, it occurs twice, once in Leviticus and once in Ezra. The central sense remains the recognition of a wrong or offense; the surrounding verse determines the specific situation.

This Greek LXX verb means “do” or “make”: it describes carrying out an action, producing something, or bringing something about. Its basic sense is broad, so the surrounding sentence determines whether it refers to an act, a work, or something created. It is common throughout the Greek Old Testament, occurring 2,880 times, which reflects its wide usefulness for describing what people do and what God or others make. Its first recorded occurrence is in Genesis 1:1, but the word’s normal meaning extends across many kinds of action.

This Greek LXX noun refers to an act or matter—that is, something done or an affair under consideration. It can point either to an action itself or to a matter being discussed, handled, or judged. The word occurs 108 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented here, so it is used broadly rather than for only one specialized kind of situation. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

gl: one who speaks in behalf of
d: one who speaks in behalf of

e.t: This noun refers to one who speaks in behalf of another. It describes a person acting as a representative in speech, rather than merely speaking in general. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 2 Maccabees 7. The word centers on speaking for someone else, while the surrounding passage determines the particular role or purpose involved. Its concise meaning is therefore best understood as describing a person who speaks on another’s behalf.

“Attentively; carefully” describes doing something with focused care rather than casually or carelessly. It is an adverb, so it tells how an action is carried out. In this Greek Old Testament occurrence, the word appears once, at Proverbs 31:25. The brief lexical sense points to deliberate attention and careful conduct, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain precisely what action it describes there.

This noun means “judicial summons”: a formal call to appear before a court or other judicial authority. It refers to an official demand for someone’s presence in a legal setting, rather than a casual invitation. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 4:14. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain the specific situation in which this summons appears.

This noun means “deception” or “cunning treachery”—a purposeful act of misleading or dealing deceitfully with someone. It describes hidden dishonesty rather than an innocent mistake. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, appearing once in 2 Kings and once in Psalms. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains crafty, deliberate deceit. The word therefore points to conduct that cannot be trusted because it uses concealment or trickery against another person.

Robok, also rendered Rhovok, is a proper name referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears once, in Numbers 31:8. The name itself identifies the person; the surrounding verse and passage are needed to understand that person’s role in the account. This word should therefore be read as a personal name, not translated as a general concept or ordinary title.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Saouli” or “Sauli.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 26:13. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, the name’s precise role in that passage cannot be explained further; its established lexical function is simply to identify someone by name.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Sepphama” or “Sepfama.” It identifies a named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 34:10. Because the verse text is not available here, its specific referent cannot be described more precisely. Its meaning is therefore its designation—the name itself—rather than a concept that can be translated into an ordinary descriptive word.

This noun means “elements”: the basic constituents or components that make up something. It points to such components collectively rather than to one isolated part. In the deuterocanonical Greek corpus represented here, it occurs three times, twice in Wisdom and once in 4 Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines whether the word concerns physical constituents or another kind of ordered component, but its central sense remains the parts from which something is formed.

This Greek LXX verb means to join in reviling—taking part with others in speaking abusively or contemptuously against someone. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Jeremiah 36:27. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning centers on participating in hostile, insulting speech directed at another person.

“Take along with” means to bring or accompany someone by taking that person with you. It is a verb describing an action of including another person in one’s movement or journey, rather than leaving that person behind. In the Septuagint, it occurs three times: twice in Old Testament books and once in 3 Maccabees. The exact person being taken and the reason for going must be learned from the surrounding verse, but the word itself centers on taking someone along.

This verb means “burn to cinders”: to consume something by fire until it is reduced to charred remains. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at Isaiah 42:25. The word’s basic sense is focused and forceful, portraying thorough burning rather than a light scorching or warming. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This LXX noun refers to a sharp, expressive sound—either “hissing” or “bleating.” It can describe the noise made by people or animals, depending on the surrounding passage. The word appears four times in the Greek Old Testament and related writings, with both senses represented. Its basic idea is not a spoken message but a noticeable sound that communicates distress, rejection, fear, or animal noise through its context.

This Greek LXX noun means “completion”: the bringing of something to its finished or complete state. It can describe an achieved end or the completion of an appointed matter. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 16 times, especially in passages connected with the regulations and offerings of Exodus and Leviticus. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being brought to completion there.

This Greek LXX noun means “enjoyment; delight”—the pleasurable satisfaction or gladness someone experiences. It can describe something that brings pleasure or the state of taking pleasure in it. The word occurs seven times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing in both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. English translations sometimes render it with “delight,” which fits its basic sense. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means to “pierce” or “perforate”—to make a hole or pass through something with a sharp object. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, once in 2 Kings and once in Job. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains the act of puncturing or making an opening through something.

This noun means “hyena,” referring to the wild animal. It identifies a creature rather than an action, quality, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs once, at Jeremiah 12:9. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains the name of this scavenging animal. It should therefore be understood as a straightforward animal reference, not as a broader description unless the verse’s context supplies one.

This Greek LXX verb means “shield”: to act as a protective defense for someone or something. It describes the action of standing between a person and danger, or covering and guarding them from harm. The word occurs 19 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including passages that speak of God as a shield. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is active protection.

Pharathōm is a proper name, rendered “Pharathōm; Farathom.” Unlike a word that describes an action, quality, or object, this term functions as a specific name rather than an ordinary descriptive expression. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs one time, at Judges 12:15. The available lexical information identifies the name but does not provide further details about whom or what it designates, so its precise referent must be determined from the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “flee”: to move away quickly from danger, pursuit, or an opposing situation. It describes escaping rather than remaining to face what threatens or presses against someone. The word occurs 220 times in this LXX corpus, across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings represented there, so it is a regularly used action word. Its precise force in any passage depends on who is fleeing and what they are leaving, but the central idea remains urgent departure or escape.

This noun means “widowhood”: the condition or status of being a widow. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Genesis 38. The word names a life situation rather than a person; a widow is the person, while widowhood describes her state after her husband’s death. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Chous, also written Khus, is a proper name used in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings. It identifies a named person or place in the passages where it occurs, rather than expressing a general action, quality, or object. The name appears 51 times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, beginning in Genesis and continuing through 1 Maccabees. Its precise referent depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “rawness,” referring to the quality or condition of being raw. It names rawness as a state or characteristic rather than describing an action. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in the deuterocanonical books of 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains the condition of being raw.

Ose, also rendered Osi, is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a personal designation rather than as a description of an action, quality, or object. The name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in Numbers and 1 Chronicles. The available lexical information identifies the name but does not provide a further word meaning or explain its origin. Its precise identity in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.
